newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Rushdie tells EU to show "teeth" against Iran fatwa.
newsitem.headline: Rushdie tells EU to show "teeth" against Iran fatwa.

text.p: British author Salman Rushdie told the European Union on Tuesday that its attempts to lift an Iranian death threat hanging over him had been largely ineffective and needed "teeth" to make them worthwhile.
The Iranian death edict or fatwa was issued in 1989 by Iran's then spiritual leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomenei because of alleged blasphemy against Islam in Rushdie's novel "The Satanic Verses".
Rushdie was forced into hiding and the EU began what it calls a "critical dialogue" with Iran to get the fatwa lifted.
"After almost eight years I am beginning to get impatient," Rushdie told reporters before a meeting in Dublin with Irish foreign minister Dick Spring, representing the EU.
Ireland is currently EU president and Iran said in July the Irish presidency was an ideal opportunity to resolve the situation. But Rushdie said little progress had been made.

"I do think that the critical dialogue has been largely ineffective and one of the reasons for that is it seems to have very few teeth," he said. "I"m interested in ways in which teeth can be inserted into the process."

Spring said the EU remained committed to getting the ruling lifted. "The threats under which Mr Rushdie lives are not acceptable to the EU and it is our responsibility to do anything we can to make sure the fatwa is lifted at the earliest possible time," he told reporters.
He conceded that the EU's approach had borne little fruit so far but said dialogue was still considered the best way forward.
"The success has not been great to put it quite honestly, but at the same time we feel it's worth pursuing and will be continuing with our discussions."

Spring said alternative approaches like cutting off contact and isolating Iran could have even less chance of getting the fatwa lifted. The U.S. wants its European allies to cut off all links with Iran, which it regards as a sponsor of terrorism.

"The balance of opinion at present is that the critical dialogue is at least a form of contact," Spring said "Even though the results from the dialogue have been very few and far between, would you get any results from the alternatives?"
But he said the EU remained divided over policy toward Iran and its policy could change if the balance of opinion shifted.

Rushdie said Britain had warned him his life was still in danger. "I am happy to say that there hasn't been any sort of close attempt on my life, nobody's ever got particularly close to me," he said. "But what remains is the very serious threat from the Iranian government."

Iran says the edict is irrevocable. It has already rejected an EU request for a written declaration that it would not carry out the fatwa and would seek to restrain Iranians from trying to assassinate Rushdie. But it has said it will not send anyone to kill the author.
